newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower after rally loses steam.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower after rally loses steam.

text.p: The dollar ended lower Wednesday amid fear of a potentially troubling trade report slated for release in Japan, despite an early climb on dollar-friendly comments from Germany's finance minister.

Germany's Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the dollar and British pound had risen against the German mark because of strong economies in their respective countries and that currency market fluctuations were no grounds for worry.
"In essence, he was giving the green light to buy dollars," said John McCarthy, senior vice president at ING Barings.
The comments from Waigel and other German officials were far more optimistic than investors had expected and pushed the dollar higher.
German spokesman Peter Hausmann told a news briefing said the mark's weakness would stimulate German exports and job growth.
A weaker mark lowers relative prices of products made in Germany, making them more competitive in international markets.

"While they didn't condone the dollar's move higher, certainly the rhetoric the markets had expected from the Germans did not come out," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president for corporate foreign exchange at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
But the dollar's rally stalled at 1.80 marks, a key psychological barrier where some dealers have speculated the Bundesbank might enter the market to sell dollars for marks.
As a result, investors sold the dollar, booking healthy profits posted during its recent surge to near six-year highs.
"There was no follow-through buying, so people just dumped dollars. At 1.80 marks, that was seen as an unattractive level to own dollars," McCarthy said.
Investors also looked to lighten dollar holdings ahead of a report on Japan's customs-cleared trade data for June due for release Wednesday night.

Forecasts put Japan's trade gap at 1.1 trillion yen ($9.5 billion), a 49 percent increase from May. Such a number could trigger heavy yen buying for dollars, and investors sold dollars in anticipation, dealers said.
"With the trade figures coming out, people were a bit fearful of owning dollars. We had a large seller come into the market and we made a quick move down," said Flanagan.

The dollar fell to 1.7910 marks from 1.7935 late Tuesday and to 115.62 Japanese yen from 115.76. The British pound fell to $1.6787 from $1.6788. The dollar rose to 1.4747 Swiss francs from 1.4735 and to Canadian $1.3738 from C$1.3702.
The German comments and the dollar's modest declines eased fears of official market intervention to halt its rally, traders said.
"Intervention seems pretty unlikely at this point," said Flanagan.
Dealers said the dollar would continue to move higher in coming sessions despite short-term swings, bolstered by strong U.S. economic growth.
"At some point I think the dollar goes higher, but that doesn't mean we can't see it go down in the meantime," said McCarthy.
Data released Wednesday on consumer prices and industrial production for June offered fresh evidence of steady, low-inflation growth in the United States.
The consumer price index in the first half of 1997 rose at its slowest rate in 32 years, while manufacturing output rose 0.3 percent in June, faster than expected.
